title: st.pydeck_chart selection events (on_select="rerun") are never delivered when the chart is inside @st.fragment
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the existing issues for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`st.pydeck_chart(..., on_select="rerun", key=...)` never delivers the selection event to the server when the chart is rendered **inside a `@st.fragment`**. Clicking a pickable object does nothing: no fragment rerun, no app rerun, no selection state, no console error. Hover picking (auto_highlight + tooltip) works normally, so WebGL picking itself is alive — only the selection event pipeline is dead.

The exact same chart **outside** a fragment works perfectly.

Reproduced on **1.56.0 and 1.59.1** (Windows 11, Python 3.14, pydeck 0.9.x, Chromium via Playwright and real Chrome).

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import pydeck as pdk
import streamlit as st

hexes = ["87a8100d9ffffff", "87a8100dbffffff", "87a8100c1ffffff"]  # neighbors, São Paulo

def chart(key):
    layer = pdk.Layer(
        "H3HexagonLayer",
        data=[{"hex_id": h} for h in hexes],
        id="hexes",
        get_hexagon="hex_id",
        get_fill_color=[0, 150, 255, 160],
        pickable=True,
        auto_highlight=True,
    )
    deck = pdk.Deck(
        layers=[layer],
        initial_view_state=pdk.ViewState(latitude=-23.55, longitude=-46.64, zoom=9),
        map_style=None,
    )
    ev = st.pydeck_chart(deck, on_select="rerun", key=key, height=400)
    objs = getattr(getattr(ev, "selection", None), "objects", {}) or {}
    st.write(key, "->", "SELECTED_OK" if objs else "NO_SELECTION")

st.subheader("Outside fragment — clicking a hexagon WORKS")
chart("outside_fragment")

@st.fragment
def frag():
    st.subheader("Inside @st.fragment — clicking a hexagon does NOTHING")
    chart("inside_fragment")

frag()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. `streamlit run app.py`
2. Click a blue hexagon in the **first** (outside-fragment) chart → `SELECTED_OK` appears.
3. Click a blue hexagon in the **second** (inside-fragment) chart → nothing happens. No rerun (the running indicator never appears), no selection, no browser console error, no server log.

### Expected Behavior

Clicking a pickable object inside a fragment should trigger the fragment rerun and populate `event.selection.objects`, like it does outside a fragment (and like other selection-enabled elements, e.g. `st.plotly_chart`, do inside fragments).

### Current Behavior

The selection event is silently dropped. Hover highlight and tooltips keep working, which makes this quite hard to debug in a real app — the map looks alive but clicks go nowhere.

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version (our production app, whose pydeck chart has lived inside a fragment since May 2026, had working clicks on older Streamlit builds; after rebuilding with a current version the clicks died with no code change).

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.56.0 and 1.59.1 (both reproduce)
- Python version: 3.14 (also 3.11)
- Operating System: Windows 11 / Debian 13 (Docker)
- Browser: Chrome / Chromium

### Additional Information

Found while debugging a production dashboard where the pydeck chart + click handler live inside `@st.fragment` for rerun-cost reasons. Removing the decorator (chart inline in the page) immediately restores click delivery — that is our current workaround.

title: Add a developer debug pane for inspecting state, cache, memory, and profiling
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a built-in developer "debug pane" — a panel (e.g. a collapsible sidebar/overlay) that surfaces debug information and dev tools without cluttering the main app. It would visualize `st.session_state` and cache contents, show memory usage and profiling/performance info, and provide a place to dump debug output (`st.help`, variables, etc.). By default it would be visible only to the app developer (not viewers), so developers don't have to comment debug code in and out.

### Why?

Debugging Streamlit apps today means peppering the main UI with `st.write(st.session_state)`, `st.help(...)`, timing prints, etc., then remembering to remove them. There's no first-class way to inspect what's actually going on — state, cache, memory, timings — in a dedicated, developer-only surface. A debug pane (à la [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar)) would make development and troubleshooting dramatically easier and keep debug output out of the real app for end users.

### How?

A developer-only container/panel that is disabled by default for viewers other than the app developer. Over time it could host focused tools, for example:

- **State inspector:** visualize `st.session_state` contents.
- **Cache inspector:** visualize `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource` contents (and allow clearing).
- **Memory profiling:** memory usage, and how it changes run-over-run.
- **Execution/performance profiling:** time between/within widget calls and functions; distribution of run times run-over-run (e.g. via a profiler like yappi + a viewer like snakeviz).
- **Debug output container:** a scratch area to write `st.help`, dump variables, etc., that doesn't appear in the main window.
- **Variable inspector:** e.g. a selectbox + `st.help`.
- **Element/DOM inspector:** which widgets were rendered, and their inputs/values; last forward/back message (or equivalent).
- **Console logs** and **error context**.
- Possibly a **Python console** at the end of the app to run quick calculations/inspections (like a Jupyter interactive debugger).

Considerations:
- Developer-only visibility by default (not shown to app viewers); tie into a development vs. production mode.
- Start minimal (state + cache inspection) and grow over time.

### Additional Context

- Prior art: [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar), [streamlit-forum](https://github.com/snehankekre/streamlit-forum).
- Closely related: #16306 (dedicated development and production modes) — this debug pane is a natural home for the "development mode" dev tools described there.

title: Add a link/bookmark element that renders a rich link preview card
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a link/bookmark element that renders a URL as a rich preview card — with properties like an icon/favicon, title, description, and optionally a preview image — similar to how a bookmark looks in Notion or a link result in Google search. It could optionally **auto-fetch** these properties (e.g. from the page's Open Graph / metadata) when they aren't provided explicitly, and it should **adapt its layout** based on which properties are present.

### Why?

Links are everywhere in apps (sources, references, related resources, docs), but a bare Markdown link is visually flat. A rich, consistent link/bookmark card makes references look polished and scannable — great for dashboards, research/agent apps that cite sources, resource lists, and "read more" sections. Today users hand-build these with columns + images + markdown or custom components, which is fiddly and inconsistent.

### How?

A new element, e.g.:

```python
st.link_preview(
    "https://streamlit.io",
    title="Streamlit • A faster way to build and share data apps",
    description="Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for data scientists and AI/ML engineers to deliver interactive data apps – in only a few lines of code.",
    icon="https://streamlit.io/favicon.png",   # icon/favicon
    image="https://.../preview.png",           # optional large preview image
)

# Minimal — auto-fetch metadata from the URL:
st.link_preview("https://streamlit.io")
```

Behavior:
- **Dynamic layout:** adapt the card to whichever properties are provided — e.g. compact (favicon + title + description) vs. a larger card with a preview image (like the two reference looks below).
- **Auto-fetch (optional):** when title/description/icon/image aren't given, fetch them from the target URL's metadata (Open Graph / `<meta>` / favicon). Should be opt-in-friendly and degrade gracefully if fetching fails or is blocked (fall back to just the URL/title). Consider caching and the SiS/Community-Cloud implications of server-side fetching (and whether fetching happens backend- or frontend-side).
- Whole card is a link to the URL; supports opening in a new tab.

**Alternative / complementary: a Markdown directive.** This could also be exposed as a Markdown directive so bookmarks can be embedded inline in any markdown text (e.g. `st.markdown`), for example:

```
:bookmark[https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/toc/]{title="Foo" icon=":material/info:"}
```

The directive attributes (`title`, `description`, `icon`, `image`, …) map to the same properties as the element, and unspecified ones can be auto-fetched. A directive plays nicely with LLM-generated content and lets bookmarks appear inline within larger blocks of text.

**Simpler inline "mentions".** The same directive family could also cover a lighter-weight inline link — not a full card, but a link that doesn't use the default link color and instead has a more button-like hover effect, with a configurable icon and title. For example:

```
:mention[URL]{text="My link"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="🍀"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="github"}
:mention[URL]{icon="streamlit"}
```

This gives a compact, chip/mention-style link (great inline in text or chat) that sits between a plain Markdown link and the full bookmark card.

Reference looks (a compact link result vs. a larger card with a preview image):

- Compact: favicon + site + bold title (link color) + description snippet.
- Rich: title + description on the left, with a preview image on the right and favicon + URL at the bottom.

### Additional Context

- Inspired by link/bookmark cards in Notion and rich link results in Google search.
- Complements a possible OEmbed feature (embedding Streamlit content elsewhere); this is the inverse — richly embedding external links inside a Streamlit app.
- Related: #11990 (file chip element, e.g. for `st.chat_message`) — a similar compact, reference-style element that could share design/infrastructure.

title: Deprecate widget callback `args`/`kwargs` in favor of `functools.partial`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Deprecate the `args` and `kwargs` parameters that widgets currently expose for passing arguments to `on_change` / `on_click` callbacks, and recommend `functools.partial` instead. As part of this, support automatically receiving relevant state (e.g. the widget's new value) in the callback, as requested in #5305.

### Why?

- **Redundant API surface:** `args`/`kwargs` exist on essentially every widget purely to forward arguments to callbacks. Python already has a standard, well-understood tool for this — `functools.partial` — so `args`/`kwargs` are extra parameters to learn, document, and maintain on every widget for something the language handles natively.
- **Consistency & simplicity:** removing them shrinks the signature of every widget and aligns with "prefer Pythonic idioms" and "extend/compose over inventing".
- **Better ergonomics for callbacks:** today callbacks often have to read `st.session_state` to find out what value changed, which makes generic reusable handlers awkward. Passing the value (and possibly key) to the callback automatically (#5305) removes that friction.

### How?

- **Recommend `functools.partial`** as the replacement for `args`/`kwargs`:

```python
from functools import partial

def update(param_name, *, value):
    ...

st.selectbox("Pick", options, on_change=partial(update, "selection_1"))
```

- **Deprecate `args`/`kwargs`** on widgets with a long, clearly-communicated deprecation window and docs/migration guidance (they keep working during the deprecation period). See API principle "Graceful Evolution" (3+ months notice, clear migration path).
- **Auto-pass state to callbacks** (#5305): make the widget's new value available to the callback automatically (e.g. as a keyword argument), so reusable/generic handlers don't need to reach into `st.session_state`. The exact mechanism needs design (opt-in signature detection vs. a fixed kwarg) to stay backwards compatible.

### Additional Context

- Incorporates #5305 (pass state as a parameter to the `on_change` callback).
- This is a cross-cutting change affecting all widgets with callbacks (`on_change`/`on_click`), so it warrants a spec and careful, gradual deprecation.

title: Support inline tooltips in Markdown (hover text), e.g. via a `:tooltip[...]` directive
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a way to include inline text in Markdown that shows a tooltip when hovered — like abbreviations/glossary terms with an explanation on hover. This could be exposed as a new Markdown directive, and #12474 (show footnotes as tooltips) could be generalized to cover this.

### Why?

It's common to want to annotate a word or phrase with extra context that appears on hover — glossary terms, acronym expansions, definitions, or short explanations — without cluttering the main text. Today there's no native way to do this in Streamlit Markdown; users resort to raw HTML (`<abbr>`/`title`) which is limited and not always allowed. A first-class inline tooltip makes docs, dashboards, and explanatory text much richer.

### How?

Add a Markdown directive for inline tooltips, where the bracketed text is displayed and the `text` attribute is shown on hover:

```
The :tooltip[HTML]{text="Hyper Text Markup Language"} specification...

:tooltip[Streamlit]{text="Open-source app framework for Machine Learning and Data Science teams."}
```

Notes:
- The visible text (`[...]`) renders inline; hovering shows the tooltip `text`.
- Works wherever Streamlit Markdown is rendered (`st.markdown`, `st.write`, captions, etc.).
- Consider whether the tooltip `text` itself supports Markdown.
- **Alternative / complementary:** generalize #12474 (footnotes → tooltips). Markdown footnotes could render as hover tooltips, giving a standard-Markdown path to the same result; the `:tooltip[...]` directive is the more explicit, inline alternative.

### Additional Context

- Related: #12474 (show markdown footnotes as tooltips) — this issue proposes a more generic, directive-based approach to inline hover text.

title: Support tooltips in Markdown (footnotes-as-tooltips and/or a `:tooltip[...]` directive)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a way to include text in Streamlit Markdown that shows a tooltip when hovered — for glossary terms, acronym expansions, definitions, or short explanations. There are two complementary approaches:

1. **Footnotes as tooltips:** render standard Markdown footnotes as hover tooltips.
2. **A `:tooltip[...]` directive:** an explicit inline directive for annotating a word/phrase with hover text.

### Why?

It's common to annotate a word or phrase with extra context that appears on hover, without cluttering the main text. Today there's no native way to do this in Streamlit Markdown; users resort to raw HTML (`<abbr>`/`title`), which is limited and not always allowed. First-class Markdown tooltips make docs, dashboards, and explanatory text much richer.

### How?

**Option 1 — Footnotes as tooltips.** Some Markdown parsers support footnotes (see the [Markdown guide](https://www.markdownguide.org/extended-syntax/#footnotes) or [GitHub Markdown](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax#footnotes)). What if we showed them as actual tooltips?

```python
st.markdown("""
Here is a simple footnote[^1].

[^1]: My reference.
""")
```

`remark-gfm` (already used within Streamlit) supports GFM-compatible footnotes: https://github.com/remarkjs/remark-gfm

**Option 2 — A `:tooltip[...]` directive.** A more explicit, inline approach: the bracketed text is displayed and the `text` attribute is shown on hover.

```
The :tooltip[HTML]{text="Hyper Text Markup Language"} specification...

:tooltip[Streamlit]{text="Open-source app framework for Machine Learning and Data Science teams."}
```

Notes:
- The visible text (`[...]`) renders inline; hovering shows the tooltip `text`.
- Works wherever Streamlit Markdown is rendered (`st.markdown`, `st.write`, captions, etc.).
- Consider whether the tooltip `text` itself supports Markdown.

The two options are complementary: footnotes give a standard-Markdown path (and are great for reference-style content), while the `:tooltip[...]` directive is a more explicit, inline way to attach hover text to any span.

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: Support custom LaTeX delimiters
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

An OpenAI response uses `\(` and `\)` for inline LaTeX and `\[` and `\]` for block LaTeX, but Streamlit looks for `$` and `$$`.

So the [Build a basic LLM chat app](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/tutorials/llms/build-conversational-apps#build-a-chatgpt-like-app) code doesn't give readable results if there's LaTeX present.

It would be nice if we could handle ChatGPT LaTeX by defining the delimiters.

### Why?

As a sample, here's some raw response text from ChatGPT. This doesn't render correctly, unless I call `.replace` to use the correct delimiters. So this is my workaround:

```python
response_text = r"""
Consider the function \( f(x) = x^2 \). We want to evaluate the definite integral from \( x = 1 \) to \( x = 3 \):

\[
\int_{1}^{3} x^2 \, dx
\]
"""
new_md = (
    response_text.replace(r"\[", "$$").replace(r"\]", "$$").replace(r"\(", "$").replace(r"\)", "$")
)
st.markdown(new_md)
```

But I can't work out how to implement this replacing with a streamed response and `st.write_stream` (I'm sure it's possible, just not simple).

### How?

I think the Gradio implementation is good. They have a `latex_delimiter` arg in [their Markdown component](https://www.gradio.app/docs/gradio/markdown).

It would be great if we could define these delimiters anywhere LaTeX might eventually be used, like `write()`, `write_stream()`, `markdown()`.

A more general purpose solution might be to allow a processing callback to be passed into `write_stream` that accepts and returns text, giving users a chance to call `.replace`. Although, there's no guarantee that `\` and `(` will be in the same chunk, so this is not really a reliable way to handle this unless the function is called on the full string every time, which probably has performance issues.

### Additional Context

This is not really context, but I wanted to say that I'm blown away by Streamlit so far. I can get so much done in so little time. And the docs are *chef's kiss*.

title: Pass state as parameter to `on_change` callback
body:
### Problem

Currently it seems you need to access `st.session_state` to figure out what value was selected in the `on_change` callback, but that's limiting if you'd like to create more generic functions to handle these things.

### Solution

Send the selected value (and potentially index) automatically to the `on_change` callback function.

### Additional context

This would allow doing something like:

```python
def update_params(**kwargs):
    st.experimental_set_query_params({kwargs["param_name"]: kwargs["selected_value"]})

selection = st.selectbox(
    "Select something:",
   ["Select....", "cat", "dog"],
    key="selection_1",
    # value and id get sent automatically as kwargs!
    on_change=update_params,
    kwargs={"param_name": "selection_1"},
)
```

Which is slightly nicer IMHO than having a function for every selectbox.

Let me know if this isn't clear or doesn't make sense though...

body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

The newly launched st.pdf in version 1.49 renders the PDF in streamlit. There is an option to zoom in/out, but no option to download or print the rendered PDF. This feature is useful if the user needs a copy of the PDF.

### Why?

_No response_

### How?

I've a simple workaround, taken from [streamlit-extras](https://pypi.org/project/streamlit-extras/) and it works well for me.

```python

def pdf_reader(file: str|bytes, base_url: str = '', width: int = None, height: int = 500) -> None:
    width = '100%' if width is None else f"{width}px"   
    if isinstance(file, str) and file.startswith(('http://', 'https://', 'data:application/pdf')):
        pdf_url = file
    else:
        from streamlit.runtime import Runtime
        coordinates = st._main._get_delta_path_str()
        runtime = Runtime.instance()
        pdf_url = base_url + runtime.media_file_mgr.add(file, "application/pdf", coordinates)
    html_content = f'<iframe src="{pdf_url}" style="width:{width}; height:{height}px;" type="application/pdf" frameborder="0"></iframe>'
    st.markdown(html_content, unsafe_allow_html=True)

```

_No response_

title: Add `st.column_config.DurationColumn` for timedelta / duration values
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a dedicated `st.column_config.DurationColumn` as the first-class column type for `datetime.timedelta` / `pandas.Timedelta` / Arrow duration values. It should own duration-specific display formats, `min`/`max`/`step` as timedeltas, and a real duration editor. `TimeColumn` should stay clock-of-day only; `NumberColumn` can remain the escape hatch for “treat this duration as seconds.”

### Why?

Timedelta is elapsed time (negatives, multi-day, 336 hours). That is a different type from:

- **`TimeColumn`**: clock-of-day. HTML `<input type="time">`, `min`/`max` as `datetime.time`, wraps at 24h, string sort. Read-only rendering only looks right for the narrow case of a positive duration under 24 hours (`1s` → `00:00:01`). Everything else is a silent lie (`14 days` wraps or fakes `336:00:00`; negatives have no representation). That is the same class of bug as #9751 (`1s` shown as `00:16:40`). If `TimeColumn` cannot represent a value, it should error rather than show a wrong clock time.
- **`NumberColumn`**: numeric sort and printf formats. Good enough as a v1 for display + sort (#8949), including `format="clock"` for an elapsed-time clock. It is a leaky API for durations: `min`/`max`/`step` are raw seconds, and the editor is a number spinner on `7200`.

A dedicated type is what pays off once we want a real duration API: discoverable config, a format namespace that is not a number format, timedelta-typed bounds, and an editor that is not “type 7200 to mean 2 hours.”

### How?

```python
st.dataframe(
    df,
    column_config={
        "latency": st.column_config.DurationColumn(
            format="duration",  # humanize, default
            min_value=datetime.timedelta(0),
            max_value=datetime.timedelta(days=14),
            step=datetime.timedelta(seconds=1),
        ),
        "runtime": st.column_config.DurationColumn(format="clock"),
    },
)
```

**Default mapping:** Arrow duration / pandas timedelta → `DurationColumn` (read-only until editing ships). Keep `NumberColumn` as the opt-in for numeric / printf formats on seconds.

**Do not reuse `TimeColumn`.** Do not send nanosecond ticks to JS (overflows `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` after ~104 days). Wire format should stay **seconds as a float**; Python applies `pd.Timedelta(seconds=value)` so pandas writes the column’s native unit (`us` on pandas 3, `ns` on pandas 2). Strings can stay as a fallback (`pd.Timedelta("2 hours")`).

**Editing, in order of cost / quality:**

1. **Text parse (best first editor).** Overlay is a text field. Accept the same strings pandas already understands: `"2 hours"`, `"1 day 03:00:00"`, `"00:00:01"`, `"P2DT3H"`, `"-3 days"`. Display can stay humanized or clock; the committed value is still seconds (or a normalized string). Handles negatives and multi-day.
2. **Custom elapsed-time overlay (best UX).** Glide custom cell: optional days + `HH:mm:ss`, hours not wrapped at 24, optional sign. `min`/`max`/`step` are timedeltas. This is the main reason for `DurationColumn` to exist rather than piggyback on `NumberColumn`.
3. **Number + unit.** Spinner plus s/min/h/d. Fine as a power-user option, poor as the default for mixed-scale columns.
4. **`NumberColumn(disabled=False)`.** Already works as an escape hatch (edits raw seconds). Not product-quality as the default editor.

Suggested `format` values (duration namespace, not number formats): `"duration"` (humanize, default), `"clock"` (elapsed clock, hours not wrapped at 24), `"localized"` (Intl.DurationFormat), maybe ISO `PT2H` later.

### Additional Context

Related:

- #8949 — timedelta sort used the humanized string (`14 days`, `2 hours`, `a day`) instead of the underlying value. Fixed by mapping duration → `NumberColumn` with values stored as seconds.
- #9751 — `TimeColumn` on `pd.Timedelta` showed a wrong clock time. `TimeColumn` should keep erroring on duration; the clock display belongs on `DurationColumn` / `NumberColumn(format="clock")`.

Display + numeric sort do not require this type. Add `DurationColumn` when we want first-class editing or a cleaner public API.

title: A custom component cannot own the `r` or `c` keys: the app-level shortcuts fire regardless
body:

A custom component that binds those keys cannot keep them: even a capture-phase listener calling `preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()` and `stopImmediatePropagation()` sees the key and the app still acts on it. This makes single-letter keyboard interfaces — the norm in accessible visualization libraries, where a blind user drives a chart from the keyboard — impossible to build on Streamlit's non-iframe component path. ### Reproducible Code Example ```Python # app.py import streamlit as st st.session_state["runs"] = st.session_state.get("runs", 0) + 1 st.write(f"RUNS={st.session_state['runs']}") st.text_input("a text input") st.button("a button") st.markdown( '
' "a custom widget
", unsafe_allow_html=True, ) ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. Save the snippet above as `app.py` and run `streamlit run app.py`. 2. Click the bordered div to focus it, press r, and watch `RUNS` increment. 3. To confirm a component cannot defend the key, run this in the browser console and press r again with the div focused: ```js document.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'r') { e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); e.stopImmediatePropagation(); } }, true); // capture phase — the earliest a listener can run ``` ### Expected Behavior A component should be able to opt out of app-level key handling for the region it owns, or the exemption should extend to focus inside a registered custom component. ### Current Behavior The capture-phase listener above receives the event, and the app reruns anyway. Measured on **Streamlit 1.61.1**, driving a real browser and checking whether the app acted: | focused element | `r` | `c` | |---|---|---| | page body | app acts | app acts | | `
` | **app acts** | **app acts** | | `

title: Dialog is re-executed if `st.rerun` is triggered in an `if` statement that uses the return val from an `st.button`.
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

In a dialog, if `st.rerun` is placed behind an `if` block, in certain cases it will cause the entire dialog to be re-run instead of immediately closing it.

This only occurs when there's a button present and it's return value is _evaluated_ in an `if` statement's conditional.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
from time import sleep
import streamlit as st

@st.dialog("Expensive operation occurring...")
def non_dismissible_dialog():
    st.write("Hang tight for a few seconds...")

    # Not strictly necessary to re-produce bug. Just makes its effects more apparent.
    with st.empty():
        for x in range(1, 4):
            st.write(f"{x}...")
            # imagine we're doing some work here.
            sleep(1)
    st.write("All Done!")
    pressed = st.button( "Yay")
    if pressed:
        st.rerun()


# Again, not strictly necessary but makes the bug more apparent by not just immediately re-invoking the dialog.
pressed = st.button("See the bug")
if pressed:
    non_dismissible_dialog()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run app: `streamlit main.py`
2. click button to display dialog
3. Once available, click button to close dialog
4. Dialog re-runs.

### Expected Behavior

Instead of the dialog re-running, it should immediately close.

### Current Behavior

The dialog re-runs and the simulated heavy work inside of the dialog is re-executed.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.51.0
- Python version: 3.11.10
- Operating System: macOS Sonoma 14.7.6 (23H626)
- Browser: Chrome (142.0.7444.162)


### Additional Information

Our use-case involves a non-dismissible dialog where we provide user feedback during a heavy workload.

After the work is completed, we show the user the result and allow them to click a `Close` button, and the dialog re-running the workload is disruptive.

There is a work-around that can be used by placing a conditional inside of `st.session_state` like so:

```
@st.dialog("example")
def example_dialog():
    if st.session_state.get("example_early_exit_key", None) is None:
        st.session_state["example_early_exit_key"] = "example_value"
    else:
        st.session_state["example_early_exit_key"] = None
        st.rerun()

    # continue dialog execution as normal
```

I'm not sure how reliable that work-around is tho and I don't want to put it into production if avoidable.

title: Callback state change issue on date widget
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [X] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

I tried searching for comparable issues using: ```is:issue is:open callback -label:type:enhancement``` but I could not find a direct match..

The issue I'm running into is that the callback function on the datepicker widget fires when the state is set programmatically _using `datetime`_. So pretty much all the input fields in the datepicker widget accept `datetime` and implicitly cast them to `date`. This is fine behavior and just works. But when setting the underlying state it gives a problem, when setting the underlying state to a date programmatically the callback does not fire. This is correct behavior in my opinion. The callback should only fire when actually using the input widget. But when setting the underlying state to a `datetime`, it's cast to a `date` _and_ the callback fires. I'm guessing it's caused by the cast?

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-7216)

```Python
import datetime as dt
import streamlit as st


def updated():
    if st.session_state.get("thingy"):
        st.write(st.session_state.thingy)
    st.write(dt.datetime.now())


def update_value():
    # Uncomment/comment the below lines to go from correct to incorrect behavior
    # st.session_state.thingy = st.session_state.thingy + dt.timedelta(days=1)
    st.session_state.thingy = dt.datetime.now()


def main():
    st.title("reproducible")
    st.date_input("thingy", key="thingy", on_change=updated)
    st.button("update thingy", on_click=update_value)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```


### Steps To Reproduce

Click the button. The callback fires even though the user does not click the datepicker.

### Expected Behavior

I would expect the callback not to fire when setting it's state programmatically.. This is indeed the behaviour when setting the state to a `date` but when setting it to a `datetime` the callback fires.

### Summary

st.slider and st.number_input handles 'value' outside of the interval defined by ('min_value', 'max_value') differently. st.slider expands the interval such that 'value' is included in the interval, f.ex. if 'min_value' is 1, 'max_value' is 10 and 'value' is 12, then the slider has the interval (1, 12) instead of (1, 10). st.number_input on the other hand throws and exception when 'value' is outside of the interval ('min_value', 'max_value').

title: Sort by column value for timedelta uses string representation rather than underlying value
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [X] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [X] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Similar to #7672, sorting a timedelta column of a st.dataframe of st.data_editor does not work, because it uses the formatted string representation rather than the underlying value. Sorting by string representation leads to unnatural results because streamlit uses human readable formats. [14 days, 2 hours, 3 days, a day] is the result of ascending order rather than [2 hours, a day, 3 days, 14 days].

Ordering by formatted string can make sense for other data types (for example categorical strings such as tags), but for timedelta this is definitely not what the user expects.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-8949)

```Python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(dict(timedelta=[pd.Timedelta(hours=2),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=1),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=3),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=14)]))

st.dataframe(df)
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Click on column header 'timedelta' to explicitly sort the values ascendingly.


### Expected Behavior

Nothing should happen because the values are already sorted ascendingly. The values should be sorted by their underlying timedelta values, here: [2 hours, a day, 3 days, 14 days].

### Current Behavior

The values are sorted by their string representation: [14 days, 2 hours, 3 days, a day].

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version:  1.35.0
- Python version:  3.11.5
- Operating System: MacOs
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

This problem can be worked around by using a total seconds representation. Fully fledged example is shown below. The 'timedelta' and 'timedelta_formatted' columns will not sort correctly. But 'total_seconds' and 'total_seconds_formatted' work as expected. 'total_seconds_formatted' are displayed exactly like 'timedelta', thus solves the problem with a little cognitive overhead. 

```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import functools

df = pd.DataFrame(dict(timedelta=[pd.Timedelta(hours=2),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=1),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=3),
                                  pd.Timedelta(days=14)]))

df['total_seconds'] = df['timedelta'].dt.total_seconds()

from babel.dates import format_timedelta

format_timedelta_ = functools.partial(format_timedelta, locale='en')

df['timedelta_formatted'] = df['timedelta']
df['total_seconds_formatted'] = df['total_seconds']


def format_total_seconds(td) -> str:
    return format_timedelta_(pd.Timedelta(seconds=td).to_pytimedelta())


df = df.style.format(format_timedelta_, subset=['timedelta_formatted']).format(format_total_seconds,
                                                                               subset=['total_seconds_formatted'])

st.dataframe(df)
```

title: `AppTest.switch_page()` cannot navigate to an `st.navigation` page that sets a custom `url_path`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`AppTest.switch_page(page_path)` computes the target page hash from the page's **file
name**. But `st.navigation` identifies each `st.Page` by its **`url_path`**. When a page
sets a custom `url_path` that differs from its file name, the two hashes disagree:
`switch_page` sets a `_page_hash` that matches no registered page, and the script runner
**silently falls back to the default page** instead of navigating to the requested one (and
without raising).

This makes it impossible to test navigation to any page declared like
`st.Page("other.py", url_path="custom")`.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
See below.
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Files (all in one directory):

`home.py`
```python
import streamlit as st

st.write("HOME PAGE")
```

`other.py`
```python
import streamlit as st

st.write("OTHER PAGE")
```

`app.py`
```python
import streamlit as st

home = st.Page("home.py", default=True)
other = st.Page("other.py", url_path="custom")  # url_path != file name ("other")

st.navigation([home, other]).run()
```

`test_switch_page.py`
```python
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest


def test_switch_to_page_with_custom_url_path():
    at = AppTest.from_file("app.py").run()
    assert at.markdown[0].value == "HOME PAGE"

    at.switch_page("other.py").run()

    assert at.markdown[0].value == "OTHER PAGE"  # FAILS: is "HOME PAGE"
```

Run pytest:
```
$ pytest test_switch_page.py
E       AssertionError: assert 'HOME PAGE' == 'OTHER PAGE'
```

### Expected Behavior

`at.switch_page("other.py").run()` renders the `other` page (or, if the path can't be resolved to a registered page, raises a clear error).

### Current Behavior

The default page is rendered, silently.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1
- Python version: 3.13.15
- Operating System: Linux (WSL2) — also expected on macOS/Windows; not platform-specific


### Additional Information

#### Root cause

`AppTest.switch_page` derives the hash from the file name
(`streamlit/testing/v1/app_test.py`):

```python
page_path_str = str(full_page_path.resolve())
_, page_name = page_icon_and_name(Path(page_path_str))
self._page_hash = calc_hash(page_name)          # hash of the FILE NAME
```

but `st.navigation` registers each page under a hash derived from its `url_path`
(`streamlit/navigation/page.py`):

```python
@property
def _script_hash(self) -> str:
    return calc_hash(self._url_path)             # hash of the URL PATH
```

`self._url_path` defaults to the file-name-derived slug, so the two hashes coincide **only
when `url_path` is not overridden**. With a custom `url_path`, `calc_hash(page_name)`
matches no registered page, so the runner uses the default page instead.

#### Suggested fix

Resolve the requested page against the app's registered navigation pages (via the
`PagesManager` / `st.navigation` result), matching by resolved script path, and use that
page's actual `_script_hash` (which respects `url_path`) for `_page_hash`. Because the
navigation config is only known once the app runs, this can be done by deferring resolution
to the next `run()` (store the requested path in `switch_page`, resolve it against the
freshly built pages when running).

At minimum — even without full resolution — `switch_page`/`run` should **raise a clear
error when the computed hash matches no registered page**, rather than silently rendering
the default page, so the failure is not hidden from test authors.

#### Workaround

Set `_page_hash` to the `url_path`-based hash directly for the affected pages:

```python
from streamlit.util import calc_hash

at._page_hash = calc_hash("custom")  # the page's url_path
at.run()
```

App script


title: Prevent updates of disabled inputs in `AppTest`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

It would be great, if `AppTest` would check whether an element is disabled before updating its value. Trying to do so should lead to an error or at least a warning.

### Why?

When running AppTests I sometimes stumble upon cases, where the tests work even when they shouldn't ... just for me to find out, that again I changed values of disabled elements within the tests and `AppTest` happily does that.

Having at least a warning would make it easier to find those quirks in the tests.

### How?

Nothing needs to change in the interface.

For convenience and backward compatibility it would be possible to include a flag in `AppTest` to configure the behavior, e.g. `at = AppTest('test_main.py', default_timeout=30, on_update_disabled_element='warning')`
with the possible values:
- `accept`: take the new value without complaint (default, current behavior)
- `warning`: take the new value and issue a warning
- `error`: raise an error when trying to update a disabled element

### Additional Context

Below you can find a short example to illustrate the problem: currently the test succeeds even though changing the value would not be possible in the app itself.

To run the example
- save the code as `test_main.py`
- run `pytest`

```python
import streamlit as st
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

st.text_input('Text', value='initial value', disabled=True, key='k_text')


def test_disabled_input():
    at = AppTest('test_main.py', default_timeout=30)
    at.run()

    at.text_input(key='k_text').set_value('new value')
    at.run()

    assert at.text_input(key='k_text').value == 'new value'
```

title: StreamlitInvalidColorError message renders as one run-on line because bullets lack newlines
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`StreamlitInvalidColorError` builds its message from implicitly concatenated string literals, but the literals that introduce the bullet list have no separating newline:

```python
# lib/streamlit/errors.py:589-592
"This does not look like a valid color: {color}.\n\n"
"Colors must be in one of the following formats:"
"* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`"
"* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`",
```

Python concatenates these into a single line, so the two bullets never start a new line. Because the message is rendered as Markdown, the `*` characters do not become a list — they appear as literal asterisks mid-sentence.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

st.map(
    {"lat": [37.77], "lon": [-122.4]},
    color="not-a-color",
)
```

Or directly:

```python
from streamlit.elements.lib.color_util import to_int_color_tuple

to_int_color_tuple("red")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Pass any invalid color to an API that validates colors (`st.map(color=...)`, `st.scatter_chart(color=...)`, etc.).
2. Read the resulting error message.

### Expected Behavior

```
This does not look like a valid color: 'red'.

Colors must be in one of the following formats:
* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`
* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`
```

### Current Behavior

```
This does not look like a valid color: 'red'.

Colors must be in one of the following formats:* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`
```

### Suggested Fix

Append `\n` to the `"...following formats:"` literal and to the first bullet.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The error message renders as a Markdown bullet list in the app.
- [ ] The plain-text form contains one bullet per line.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

I scanned the rest of `lib/streamlit/` for the same pattern (a string literal beginning `* ` or `- ` immediately following a literal that does not end in a newline) using a `tokenize`-based check; `errors.py:591-592` is the only occurrence, so this looks like an isolated slip rather than a systemic one.

title: is_mem_address_str() fails on uppercase hex addresses, breaking st.write() and st.help() object rendering on Windows
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`is_mem_address_str()` in `lib/streamlit/string_util.py` matches memory-address reprs with the regex `^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-f]+\>$`. The address group only accepts **lowercase** hex digits. On Windows, CPython formats object addresses with **uppercase** hex (e.g. `<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`), so the function returns `False` for essentially every real object repr on that platform.

Both callers of this helper then take the wrong branch: `st.write(obj)` stops routing plain objects to the object-help view and prints the raw memory address instead, and `st.help()` renders memory addresses as member values while dropping those members' docstrings.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st


class Foo:
    """A Foo."""

    x = 1

    @property
    def e(self):
        "Property e"
        return 5


st.write(Foo())   # expected: rich object-help view. On Windows: raw memory address as inline code.
st.help(Foo)      # expected: property `e` documented. On Windows: "<property object at 0x...>".
```

Minimal check of the helper itself:

```python
from streamlit.string_util import is_mem_address_str


class Foo:
    pass


print(repr(Foo()))                  # <__main__.Foo object at 0x0000023FFDF98AD0>
print(is_mem_address_str(repr(Foo())))          # False   <-- should be True
print(is_mem_address_str("<foo blarg at 0x15ee6f9a0>"))  # True (lowercase only)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. On Windows, run either snippet above (or just the plain-Python helper check — no browser needed).
2. Observe that `is_mem_address_str` returns `False` for a repr it is explicitly designed to detect.

### Expected Behavior

`is_mem_address_str()` should recognize a CPython memory-address repr regardless of the hex casing produced by the platform's C runtime. Consequently:

- `st.write(obj)` renders the object-help view for an object with no other special handling.
- `st.help(SomeClass)` shows the property's docstring and leaves the value slot empty rather than printing a memory address.

### Current Behavior

On Windows (verified with `AppTest`):

```
markdown elements: ['`<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`']
help elements    : 0
```

`st.help` on a class with a `@property`:

```
name='e' type='property' value='<property object at 0x000002500A1F3240>' doc=''
```

versus the same class instance, which takes the other code path and is correct:

```
name='e' type='property' value='' doc='Property e'
```

The repository's own tests catch this — they currently fail on Windows for exactly this reason:

- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_obj_instance` → `AssertionError: Expected 'help' to be called once. Called 0 times.`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html_no_html_tags_in_string`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html_not_callable`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/help_test.py::StHelpTest::test_class_members` → `assert '<property ob...>' == ''`

They pass on Linux/macOS because glibc's `%p` formatting yields lowercase hex, which is why CI has not caught it.

### Root Cause

`lib/streamlit/string_util.py:250-252`

```python
_OBJ_MEM_ADDRESS: Final = re.compile(
    r"^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-f]+\>$"
)
```

`[0-9a-f]+` cannot match `0000027B0C1B1550`.

### Suggested Fix

Accept both casings, e.g. `[0-9a-fA-F]+` (or add `re.IGNORECASE`).

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `is_mem_address_str()` returns `True` for uppercase-hex reprs such as `<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`.
- [ ] `st.write(obj)` produces a help element (not a markdown memory address) on Windows.
- [ ] `st.help(SomeClass)` no longer renders `<property object at 0x...>` and preserves property docstrings.
- [ ] A regression test covers an uppercase-hex address string so the behavior is asserted independently of the host platform.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown — the regex appears long-standing.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: n/a (reproduced headlessly via `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest` and direct function calls)

### Additional Information

The two affected call sites are `lib/streamlit/elements/help.py:482` and `lib/streamlit/elements/write.py:576`.

title: Python unit tests are not portable to Windows (path separators, NamedTemporaryFile reopen, registry-dependent MIME type)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

Running the Python unit suite on Windows produces a large number of failures that are caused by the tests themselves rather than by the library. `CONTRIBUTING.md` does not restrict development to POSIX, so a contributor on Windows currently cannot use a green suite as a baseline.

This report covers three failures whose root cause I isolated precisely. (Two other clusters are excluded on purpose: the `write_test.py` / `help_test.py` failures belong to a separate library bug I filed about `is_mem_address_str`, and the `metrics_util_test.py` cluster is caused by the tests reading the developer's real home directory, which is a distinct test-isolation concern.)

### Steps To Reproduce

```console
$ uv run pytest lib/tests/ -q
```

on Windows.

### Failures and root causes

**1. `lib/tests/streamlit/components/v2/test_component_registry.py::test_resolve_glob_pattern_direct`**

The assertion compares a native path string against a POSIX-normalized one:

```python
assert str(resolved.resolve()) == Path(test_file).resolve().as_posix()
```

`str(Path)` yields `C:\Users\...\test-pattern.js` while `.as_posix()` yields `C:/Users/.../test-pattern.js`. These coincide only on POSIX.

```
AssertionError: assert 'C:\\Users\\a...st-pattern.js' == 'C:/Users/asu...st-pattern.js'
```

Fix: compare like with like — either `.as_posix()` on both sides or `Path(...) == Path(...)`.

**2. `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/video_test.py::VideoTest::test_st_video_subtitles_path`**

The test writes to a `NamedTemporaryFile` and, while it is still open, passes its path to `st.video(...)`, which reopens it. Windows does not permit reopening a still-open `NamedTemporaryFile`:

```
PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:\\Users\\...\\tmpyltckifk.vtt'
lib\streamlit\elements\lib\subtitle_utils.py:121: PermissionError
```

Fix: close the handle (or use `delete=False` / a `TemporaryDirectory`) before handing the path to code that opens it.

**3. `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/download_button_test.py::DownloadButtonTest::test_file_object_infers_file_name_and_mime`**

The test asserts a specific MIME type for `.csv`:

```
AssertionError: assert 'application/vnd.ms-excel' == 'text/csv'
```

`mimetypes.guess_type()` consults the Windows registry (`HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT`), where `.csv` is commonly mapped to `application/vnd.ms-excel` on machines with Excel installed. The expected value therefore depends on the host's registry rather than on Streamlit.

Fix: register the expected mapping in the test (or in library setup) via `mimetypes.add_type("text/csv", ".csv")`, or assert against `mimetypes.guess_type` rather than a hard-coded string.

### Expected Behavior

`uv run pytest lib/tests/` passes on Windows, or the supported development platforms are stated explicitly in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### Current Behavior

A full run reports **59 distinct test failures (95 including subtests)**, of which the three above are cleanly attributable to non-portable test code.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The three tests above pass on Windows without weakening what they assert.
- [ ] Optionally, a Windows job in CI (even a subset) to keep the suite portable.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

Happy to split these into separate issues or open a PR for the three fixes if that is preferred.

### Summary

Hello!

When I use `st.selectbox` with an dynamic index which can be `int | None`, with the default for `accept_new_options` (so should be False), the return type includes `str`, so gives `T | str | None` instead of `T | None`...

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st
from typing_extensions import assert_type

index: int | None = None

result = st.selectbox(
    "Entity",
    [1, 2, 3],
    index=index,

)
assert_type(result, int | None)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. setup a venv with `streamlit` (1.62.0) & `pyrefly` (1.2.0)
2. run `pyrefly check ./repro-file.py`

```
ERROR assert_type(int | str | None, int | None) failed [assert-type]
  --> main.py:12:12
   |
12 | assert_type(result, int | None)

 INFO 1 error
```

Typing should be `T | None` since I have `accept_new_options=False` (the default), so the return can never be a `str` AFAIK 🤔..

title: Allow interactive resizing of `st.columns` via drag-and-drop
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `resizable: bool = False` parameter to `st.columns` that lets users resize columns by dragging the border between them. When enabled, a border indicator appears on hover between adjacent columns, and dragging adjusts their widths interactively. Resizing is purely client-side and does not trigger a rerun. Specced in [PR #14687](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687).

### Why?

Column widths in `st.columns` are static today — once set via `spec`, they can't be adjusted without changing code and rerunning. Interactive resizing helps with dashboard customization, data exploration (temporarily expand a column to see more), fine-tuning responsive layouts, and adjusting proportions live during demos/presentations. Current workarounds (layout presets via `st.selectbox`, CSS hacks in custom components, or just accepting fixed layouts) are clunky or fragile.

Related: #5003 (deactivate responsiveness of `st.columns`), #6592 (configurable column responsiveness threshold).

### How?

```python
st.columns(
    spec,
    *,
    gap="small",
    vertical_alignment="top",
    border=False,
    width="stretch",
    resizable=False,  # NEW
)
```

- `resizable=False` (default): current fixed-width behavior, no handles.
- `resizable=True`: drag the border between adjacent columns to resize.

Behavior (from the spec):
- **Hover indicator** + `col-resize` cursor over the resize area; border fades in/out (150ms).
- **Drag** resizes only the two adjacent columns; total row width is preserved (neighbor shrinks as one grows); other columns unchanged.
- **Double-click** the handle resets the adjacent pair to their original `spec` proportions.
- **Minimum width** of 64px prevents collapse; throttled updates for performance.
- **Keyboard**: Arrow Left/Right resize in 10px increments when focused.
- **Accessibility**: handles use `role="separator"`, `aria-orientation="vertical"`, `aria-valuenow/min/max`, and visible focus indicators (WCAG 2.1).
- **Touch**: drag works via touch; indicator shows on touch start.
- **Narrow viewports**: when columns stack (below `theme.breakpoints.columns`, 640px), handles are hidden and reappear when it widens.
- **State**: resized widths persist within the session (React state) and reset on refresh, a `spec`/column-count change, or stack/unstack.

### Alternatives considered (from the spec)

- `resizable: bool` (preferred) vs `resize_mode: Literal["off", "drag"]` — boolean chosen to match the existing `border=True` precedent and the binary nature of the feature; can migrate to an enum later if multiple resize modes are demanded.
- Naming: `resizable` over `adjustable` (too generic) / `flexible` (clashes with flexbox).

### Out of scope (future work)

Persist widths across sessions, snap-to-grid, per-column `min_width`/`max_width`, `on_resize` callback, and named/saveable layout presets.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #14687 — \`[spec] Allow interactive resizing of st.columns\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687) (`specs/2026-04-08-resizable-columns/product-spec.md`).

title: Guest-to-host messages are only posted to window.parent, so a same-window embed host never receives them (METRICS_EVENT is dropped)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`HostCommunicationManager.sendMessageToHost` posts only to `window.parent`. When Streamlit is
embedded such that the host code runs *in the app's own window* (an in-iframe embed
preamble/adapter, rather than in the parent frame), no guest-to-host message reaches the host,
because `window.parent` is a third-party page in this case.

`GUEST_READY` is the one exception: `openHostCommunication` additionally posts it to the app's
own window. Every other message, notably `METRICS_EVENT`, has no such path, so embedded apps
report app-load state correctly but emit **no metrics at all** to the host.

Notably, the library already assumes this topology in the opposite direction:
`receiveHostMessage` explicitly trusts same-window self-posts, with the comment
"an in-iframe embed preamble ... when there is no trusted parent frame to relay them
(`window.parent` is a third-party page)". Only the guest-to-host direction is missing it.

### Root cause

`frontend/lib/src/hostComm/HostCommunicationManager.tsx`

```ts
// :186 — parent only
public sendMessageToHost = (message: IGuestToHostMessage): void => {
  window.parent.postMessage(this.buildVersionedMessage(message), "*")
}

// :116-121 — the only same-window dispatch, GUEST_READY exclusive
if (window !== window.parent) {
  window.postMessage(this.buildVersionedMessage(guestReadyMessage), window.location.origin)
}
```

`MetricsManager` is working correctly: with `metricsUrl === "postMessage"` it takes the
`postMessageEvent` branch and calls `sendMessageToHost`. The event is built and sent: it is
simply delivered to a window the host isn't in.

### Proposed fix

Move the same-window dispatch into `sendMessageToHost` so it applies to all guest-to-host
messages, and delete the now-redundant `GUEST_READY` block in `openHostCommunication`:

```ts
public sendMessageToHost = (message: IGuestToHostMessage): void => {
  const versionedMessage = this.buildVersionedMessage(message)
  window.parent.postMessage(versionedMessage, "*")
  // An in-window embed host cannot see a post to the third-party parent.
  if (window !== window.parent) {
    // Tagged so the echo is not executed as a host command (e.g. UPDATE_HASH).
    window.postMessage(
      { ...versionedMessage, isGuestToHostEcho: true },
      window.location.origin
    )
  }
}
```

and drop the echo early in `receiveHostMessage`:

```ts
// Our own echo (see sendMessageToHost), not an inbound host command.
if ((event.data as { isGuestToHostEcho?: boolean })?.isGuestToHostEcho) {
  return
}
```

### Alternatives considered

- Retarget to `window` when embedded — rejected, breaks parent-frame hosts (above).
- Echo only `METRICS_EVENT` — narrower and avoids the collision entirely, but leaves the same
  gap for every other message type.
- Have `receiveHostMessage` ignore all self-posts — not possible; it relies on trusting them
  for host-to-guest delivery (e.g. `SET_AUTH_TOKEN`).

### Version

- Reproduced against `develop` (`frontend/package.json` 1.62.0); observed in a deployed 1.58.0
  frontend.
- Browser: Chrome 142.


### Reproducible Code Example

```Python

```

### Steps To Reproduce

https://docs.snowflake.com/en/LIMITEDACCESS/streamlit/embed-streamlit-app

1. Embed a Streamlit app in a cross-origin page, with host code running inside the app's own
   window (i.e. the host listens via `window.addEventListener("message", ...)` in the app frame,
   not in the parent).
2. Set `metricsUrl: "postMessage"` in the host config and leave `browser.gatherUsageStats` at
   its default (`true`).
3. Attach listeners in both the parent frame and the app's own window and load the app.

**Expected:** the in-window host receives `METRICS_EVENT` (`viewReport`, `updateReport`,
`pageProfile`) along with the other guest-to-host messages.

**Actual:** only the *parent* frame receives them. The in-window host receives `GUEST_READY`
and nothing else.

### Expected Behavior

When Streamlit is embedded such that the host code runs inside the app's own window (an
in-iframe embed preamble/adapter rather than code in the parent frame), the host should receive
all guest-to-host messages — including METRICS_EVENT (`viewReport`, `updateReport`,
`pageProfile`) when the host config sets `metricsUrl: "postMessage"`.

### Current Behavior

`sendMessageToHost` posts only to `window.parent`, which in the embedding case is the third-party
embedding page and not the host. So the in-window host receives nothing.

The single exception is GUEST_READY, which `openHostCommunication` additionally posts to the
app's own window. The result is that app-load/readiness signalling works, while every other
message is silently invisible to the host, most visibly METRICS_EVENT, so embedded apps report
no usage metrics at all despite `browser.gatherUsageStats` being true and `metricsUrl` being
correctly set to "postMessage".

Confirmed by attaching `message` listeners to both frames: `viewReport`, `updateReport` and
`pageProfile` all arrive at the parent frame, and only GUEST_READY arrives in the app's own
window. MetricsManager itself behaves correctly: it takes the `postMessageEvent` branch and
builds the event; the message is just delivered to a window the host is not in.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

title: Modernize Streamlit's default light and dark themes
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Refresh Streamlit's built-in default light and dark themes to feel more modern and polished out of the box — updated colors, typography, spacing, radii, and component styling — so that apps look great by default without custom theming.

### Why?

The default look is what every new app and most demos ship with, so it strongly shapes the perception of Streamlit. The current defaults feel somewhat dated compared to modern design systems (e.g. shadcn, Tailwind, Tremor, Material 3). A refreshed, cohesive default theme would make apps look more professional immediately, improve the first impression for new users, and reduce how often people reach for custom CSS/themes just to look current.

### How?

Revisit the default theme tokens and component styling for both light and dark modes, for example:

- **Color palette:** refined neutrals/grays, a more modern primary color, and better semantic colors (success/warning/error/info) with good contrast in both modes.
- **Dark mode:** ensure it's a first-class, well-balanced theme (not just an inversion) — proper surface elevations, borders, and contrast.
- **Typography:** modern default font, refined sizes/weights/line-heights and hierarchy.
- **Spacing & shape:** consistent spacing scale and slightly softer, contemporary border radii and borders.
- **Components:** cohesive styling across widgets, containers, dataframes, charts, etc.

Considerations:
- Accessibility: maintain/improve WCAG contrast in both themes.
- Backwards compatibility: this changes the look of existing apps, so consider how to roll it out (e.g. a new theme version/opt-in, migration notes) to avoid surprising users.
- Keep it fully overridable via the existing `[theme]` config.

### Additional Context

- Inspiration: modern design systems like shadcn/ui, Tailwind, Tremor, and Material 3.

title: Rerun upon events dispatched by third-party libraries
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

We sometimes need a mechanism to rerun a Streamlit app reacting to events dispatched by third-party libraries.

One example is a reactive dashboard with Firestore like [this article](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/manufacturing/building-a-mobility-dashboard-with-cloud-run-and-firestore?hl=en), where a Streamlit app keeps displaying the latest data from Firestore in real-time by re-running the app when Firestore notifies changes.

Firestore is a database that notifies changes to the subscribers, and in the case of Python client, we can deal with the notified changes by setting an `on_snapshot` callback like below.
```python
from google.cloud import firestore_v1

db = firestore_v1.Client()
collection_ref = db.collection(u'users')

def on_snapshot(collection_snapshot, changes, read_time):
  for doc in collection_snapshot.documents:
    print(u'{} => {}'.format(doc.id, doc.to_dict()))

# Watch this collection
collection_watch = collection_ref.on_snapshot(on_snapshot)

# This sample code was copied from the article above
```

As the callback is called in a different thread independent from the main thread execution, we need to wait it to be called in the main thread with a loop and get the data from the callback via a shared data structure like a Queue.
```python
from queue import Queue

q = Queue()
def on_snapshot(collection_snapshot, changes, read_time):
  for doc in collection_snapshot.documents:
    q.put(doc.to_dict())  # Put data into the Queue

# below will run in main thread
snap = st.empty()  # placeholder

while True:
  # q.get() is a blocking function. thus recommend to add timeout
  doc = q.get()  # Read from the Queue
  snap.write(doc)  # Change the UI
 
# This sample code was copied from the article above
```

However, this loop-and-multi-thread-based approach doesn't look Streamlit-ish.

At this point, let me point out that Streamlit's execution model is like React's in that an app or a component is re-executed when a user interacts with the app or the app's state changes, and this model can't handle event sources outside the framework by design.
To address this issue, React provides [`useSyncExternalStore`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore) as a first-party solution.
Based on this analogy, I think Streamlit should also provide such a solution as a first-party feature. It fills the gap between Streamlit's execution model and event-driven third-party libraries.

title: Add a `st.card` layout container
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a general-purpose `st.card` layout container — a bordered container with a coherent, built-in structure for common card content: an optional full-width image at the top, a title (and help tooltip), and any elements you add to the body. Like `st.container(border=True)`, but with first-class support for the pieces that are painful today (especially a full-bleed image).

### Why?

Cards are one of the most common UI building blocks (see [Material design cards](https://m3.material.io/components/cards/overview)) and are everywhere in dashboards, galleries, and BI apps. Borders on `st.container`/`st.columns` are already used in a significant number of apps, so demand is clearly high. Today users can get a border via `st.container(border=True)`, but the very common "full-sized image at the top of the card" requires fragile CSS hacks. A dedicated element makes polished cards a one-liner and pairs great with grid/flex layouts and `height="stretch"` for aligned galleries.

### How?

A container command that returns a container you can fill with any elements, plus a few high-value built-in parameters (from the internal spec):

```python
st.card(
    title: str | None = None,
    image: "same types as st.image" | None = None,
    *,
    width: "content" | "stretch" | int = "stretch",
    height: "content" | "stretch" | int = "content",
    help: str | None = None,
)

# Example
with st.card("Card 1", "mountain.jpg"):
    with st.container(direction="horizontal"):
        st.badge("Star", icon=":material/star:")
        st.badge("Home", icon=":material/home:")
    st.write("This is a card with a border. It can also have some text.")
```

Details:
- Returns a container, so users add arbitrary content (text, charts, badges, buttons) to the body.
- `image` is optional and shown full width at the top (no padding, no toolbar), rendered at its natural aspect ratio; `title` is optional (Markdown, ellipsized so side-by-side cards align), with an optional `help` tooltip.
- Both `image` and `title` can be `None` (an empty card ≈ `st.container(border=True)`).
- `width`/`height` mirror `st.container`; `height="stretch"` lets cards in a row/grid align to equal height.

Possible later additions (kept out of scope initially to limit API surface): `subtitle`, `icon`/avatar, `image_height`, background color, and clickable cards.

### Additional Context

- Framed as a general card component (the internal spec called it "Image cards" because the full-sized top image was the main missing capability).
- Related: #12418 (container background / cards), #12301 (container shadow), #3210 and #4175 (older card requests), #12322 (clickable metric actions).

title: Ability to set background of st.container (or perhaps support for cards)
body: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests. - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary We should be able to set the background color of a container (preferably in a fully-themable way) ### Why? When building a dashboard with elements of different shapes and sizes placed in a grid, a nice way to align the elements visually is by making the grid structure visible. Today this is done by setting `border=True` in the grid cells (`st.container`, `st.columns`, etc). This can work well at times, but other times those borders make the app too busy visually. (Or, to combat this, the developer makes the border colors fainter, but then the app loses its "shape" and becomes harder to parse) To solve this, one thing I found works well is to set the background color of the grid cells to a different value (usually white). **Here's an example of a sad dashboard with borders:** **And here's how it looks with white cells:** ### How? As with all API proposals, ignore the exact names used below. These proposals are more about the shape of the API than the exact tokens used. ### Idea 1: Cards Introduce a new st command (`st.card`): ```py with st.card(): ... ``` ```toml # config.toml [theme] cardBackgroundColor = "#ffffff" ``` ### Idea 2: Backgrounds in containers and columns Add a new boolean property to containers and columns, following the pattern already used for turning borders on/off: ```py with st.container(filled=True, border=True): ... with st.columns(2, filled=True, border=True): ... ``` ```toml # config.toml [theme] filledContainerBackgroundColor = "#ffffff" ``` ### Idea 3: Containers with importance levels This is similar to idea 2, but here we're have a string property that follows the `kind=` pattern already used in `st.button`: ```py with st.container(type="primary", border=True): ... with st.columns(2, type="primary", border=True): ... ``` ```toml # config.toml [theme] primaryContainerBackgroundColor = "#ffffff" ``` ### Idea 4: Containers with inline background color We could just allow users to pass the background color inline as a keyword argument. I'm not a fan of this idea at the moment since it can make apps hard to maintain, while also making it harder to share themes within a company, but I'm including it here for completeness: ```py with st.container(background_color="#ffffff", border=True): ... with st.columns(2, background_color="#ffffff", border=True): ... ``` ### Additional Context _No response_

title: Configure the cookie expiration time for authentication
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

We're soon launching native authentication in Streamlit (see https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/8518). The cookie we set to keep a user logged in currently expires after 30 days. We should add a way to configure that. 

### Why?

Configuring the expiration time is good for two reasons:
1. For low-security apps, it might not matter too much how long users stay logged in, so devs might want to set a longer expiration time or disable the expiration, so users don't need to log in again. 
2. For high-security apps, devs might want to make their users log in more often, e.g. every single day. 

### How?

Should probably add a parameter like `cookie_expiration` or `cookie_ttl` to the existing `[auth]` section in `secrets.toml`. This could take the number of days or maybe even any time string (similar to what we do in a few other places). Might also be nice to be able to set this to `None` or `"never"` to not expire the cookie.

title: Configurable column responsiveness width threshold
body:
### Problem

We are using wide layout with multiple columns, and finding that our dashboard is not responsive enough on smaller screens, e.g. when moving window to laptop monitor from 4K external monitor. The columns stay in a horizontal row even when their content is very squished up, and only flex into a vertical arrangement when the screen is almost phone sized, at which point the content is still too squished to be useful.

This is particularly a problem when you have tables in columns, because the tables will overflow into the next column if the screen is not wide enough, causing overlapping content.

### Solution

Allow the width threshold for columns to be configured so that we can tune it to work better on different screen sizes used by our users, who are never going to be using phones, but do use laptop screens and wide or extra wide external monitors.

If a column contains a table, that column should not shrink further than normal soft wrapping allows, and should not overflow outside the column. Instead, the columns should wrap so that they are arranged vertically, avoiding the need to squash or overflow the table.

### Additional context

The HTML for columns generated by Streamlit uses a div that has a style attribute for flex properties rather than using a class, so we can't even override the CSS class definition to customise the flex behaviour.

title: Provide methods to refresh caching
body:
### Problem

Parts of my dashboard require sourcing CSV files from external hosts, and it can take a long time (60s) to download and processes that data. However, the data is made available at 6am every day. I already have a function which uses streamlit cache around my data fetching, but it would be amazing if I could say "at 6:05am every day, call this function".

### Solution

**MVP:** Streamlit should have a decorator you can apply to functions so they run at startup. These functions could make use of existing python scheduling libraries like apscheduler to call (and thus refresh) caching whenever needed.

**Possible additions:** Streamlit could extend its decorators, integrating the scheduling side through decorator parameters and abstracting that away from the user.

### Additional context

FR raised from this forum post: https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/eagerly-execute-specific-functions-on-app-launch/34957

It seems a few people have been trying to figure out how to refresh caching, and it would be good to not have to use selenium to simulate a web request from an external service to do so.
